p: The writer of 2 John, with the same title and nearly the same opening line.
b: "The Elder" (ho presbyteros) opens both 2 and 3 John, and "whom I love in truth" follows in both. The notes on 2 John 1:1 explain the title and the old question whether he was John the apostle or Papias' "presbyter John." Plummer drew the simple conclusion that the writer usually called himself this, and that the two letters were written at about the same time.

p: One of the most common Roman names. Four other men named Gaius appear in the New Testament.
b: Gaius was a very common name, and Plummer thought it idle to guess whether this Gaius is the Macedonian of Acts 19:29, Gaius of Derbe (Acts 20:4), or the Gaius of Corinth whom Paul baptized and who was "host to me and to the whole church" (1 Corinthians 1:14; Romans 16:23). The letter shows a believer able to house and supply traveling teachers (1:5-8), probably one of the Elder's converts (1:4), and apparently not a member of Diotrephes' church, since the Elder has to tell him what Diotrephes is doing (C. H. Dodd). The Apostolic Constitutions, written about 380, list "Of Pergamus, Gaius" among the first bishops, a late tradition that Dodd says has no early support.

p: Agapētos, "beloved, dear," is how the Elder addresses Gaius in 1:1, 1:2, 1:5 and 1:11.
b: Agapētos is the adjective from agapē, "love." The Elder calls Gaius "the beloved" and then addresses him as "Beloved" three times, each time at the start of a new section (1:2, 1:5, 1:11). 1 John uses the same address to its readers, and Jude does too (Jude 1:3: "Beloved, I was very eager to write to you"). The Plain keeps "beloved" every time, as the site's terms do.

a: in every way you are doing well
p: Euodoomai first meant "have a good journey," then simply "get on well." The KJV's "prosper" sounds like money.
b: Euodousthai comes from eu, "well," and hodos, "road." Plummer says the idea of a journey had dropped out of ordinary use; the word meant to get on well, succeed. Paul uses it twice: he prays he may "succeed in coming to you" (Romans 1:10), and each believer is to set aside "whatever he has had success earning" (1 Corinthians 16:2). The KJV's "I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper" has made this verse a favorite of the prosperity gospel (see the chapter page). Two points of the Greek matter. Peri pantōn means "in every way, concerning all things," not "above all things" (Plummer). And the same verb is used of the soul: the Elder wants Gaius' outward life to go as well as his inner life already does.

t: The ordinary health wish of a letter
p: Greek letters of the time often began, "Before all else I pray for your health." The Elder uses the form.
b: Letters on papyrus from Egypt show the form. In a letter of recommendation of about AD 25, Theon writes to Tyrannus: "Before all else I pray for your health" (Greek pro de pantōn hygiainein se euchomai, Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 292). 3 John has the same words, "I pray" (euchomai), "you" and "be in good health" (hygiainein), with "concerning all things" (peri pantōn) for Theon's "before all" (pro pantōn). The Elder takes the common wish and adds his own turn: "just as your soul is doing well." Plummer saw the verse as good authority for praying for the bodily health and success of friends.

p: Psychē is the inner self, the life of a person. The Elder contrasts it with Gaius' outward affairs.
b: Psychē can mean a person's life, self or inner being. Here it stands at the end of the sentence, set against "in every way" at the start (Plummer): Gaius' soul is already doing well; the Elder prays the rest of his life will match it. The verse does not split body from soul in the later Greek way; it simply wishes Gaius well in every part of life.

p: Adelphoi is "brothers," a word for fellow believers that includes women. Here it means traveling believers.
b: Adelphoi, plural of "brother," is the New Testament's word for fellow believers, and the plural includes women ("brothers and sisters"); the site writes "brothers," as in Acts and Romans. In 3 John the word has a narrower sense: believers traveling for the good news (1:5, 1:10) who came back to the Elder's church and told what Gaius had done for them (1:6). The Greek has no article ("when brothers kept coming"): more than one group came.

t: Testimony: a key word of 3 John
p: "Testify" and "testimony" come five times in this short letter, as they run through the Gospel of John.
b: Martyreō, "testify, give testimony," appears in 1:3, 1:6 and twice in 1:12, and "testimony" (martyria) once in 1:12. The Gospel of John is full of the same words (John 1:7: "This man came for testimony"). In 3 John testimony is how churches knew whom to trust: brothers testify to Gaius' truth, to his love before the church, and the Elder testifies for Demetrius. "Your truth" here means Gaius' faithful life, as the next words explain: "you do walk in truth" (Plummer).
orig: μαρτυρούντων σου τῇ ἀληθείᾳ (martyrountōn sou tē alētheia)

p: The Elder calls the believers in his care his children: those he brought to faith, or those he leads.
b: Ta ema tekna is emphatic: "my own children." Paul uses the same picture of converts: "It was in Christ Jesus, through the good news, that I fathered you" (1 Corinthians 4:15; compare Philemon 1:10). The Elder may mean that Gaius came to faith through him, or more broadly the members of the churches in his care (Plummer). 1 John addresses all its readers as "little children."

p: Literally "you do a faithful thing, whatever you work for the brothers." Two readings of "faithful."
b: Piston poieis is unusual Greek. Most read it as "you act faithfully," as a believer should (the Latin fideliter facis, followed by Wycliffe, Tyndale, Luther and the KJV). Westcott, as Plummer reports him, rendered it "thou makest sure whatsoever thou workest": such work will not be lost. The second verb, ergazomai, "work," is the one used in 2 John 1:8 ("what we worked for").

p: Gaius took in brothers he had never met. Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty for Jews and Christians alike.
b: The brothers were "strangers at that" (kai touto xenous): Gaius did not know them. Abraham ran to meet three strangers and fed them (Genesis 18:2-5), the model of hospitality for Jews and Christians. The Mishnah keeps the saying of Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem: "Let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household" (Avot 1:5). Paul tells the Romans, "Chase after hospitality to strangers" (Romans 12:13), and Jesus says, "When I was a stranger, you took me in" (Matthew 25:35).

p: The brothers reported to a gathering, probably the Elder's own church, not Diotrephes'.
b: "Church" (ekklēsia) appears only in 3 John among the three letters of John, here and in 1:9-10. The church of 1:6 is where the brothers told their story, most likely the Elder's own congregation; Plummer suggests Ephesus. The church of 1:9-10 is another, where Diotrephes leads. Gaius seems to belong to a third, or at least not to Diotrephes' (C. H. Dodd). The letter shows a network of house churches linked by travelers and letters.

t: "Send them on": paying for the next leg
p: Propempō meant more than a goodbye: it meant giving travelers food, money and help for the road.
b: Propempō is the word the New Testament uses for a church's support of travelers: "The church sent them on their way" (Acts 15:3); Paul hopes "to be sent on by you" to Spain (Romans 15:24); "Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey with care, so that they are short of nothing" (Titus 3:13). "In a way worthy of God" is the phrase of 1 Thessalonians 2:12 ("walk in a way worthy of God"): treat them as God's own messengers. The Didache, on the other hand, says a traveling apostle should take only bread when he leaves, and that one who asks for money is a false prophet (Didache 11).
orig: προπέμψας ἀξίως τοῦ θεοῦ (propempsas axiōs tou theou)

p: No name is given. As Jews spoke of God as "the Name," the first Christians spoke of Jesus' name the same way.
b: Hyper tou onomatos, "for the sake of the Name," is the phrase of Acts 5:41: the apostles left the Sanhedrin "glad at heart, because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name." Plummer notes that this way of speaking was common among the next generation of Christian writers (Ignatius, Clement of Rome, Hermas). In the Torah "the Name" already stands for God's own name, YHWH (Leviticus 24:11: "spoke the Name with contempt"), and Jews still say ha-Shem, "the Name." 3 John is the only New Testament book that never says "Jesus" or "Christ"; "the Name" is the only place he is named at all.

a: they take nothing from the Gentiles
p: Ethnikoi means non-Jews, here non-believers. The brothers would not live off the people they preached to.
b: Ethnikoi, "Gentiles," is Matthew's word for outsiders (Matthew 5:47; Matthew 18:17). Here it can hardly mean Gentile believers, since nothing would be wrong with taking their help; it means pagans (Plummer). The brothers set out with nothing and would not take support from those they preached to, so they depended on believers like Gaius. Jesus had sent the Twelve with "no bread, no bag, no copper coins in their belts" (Mark 6:8), and Paul worked with his own hands so as not to be a burden. Some read the clause differently, that the brothers went out "from the Gentiles," driven out with nothing, but Plummer judged the Greek against it.
orig: μηδὲν λαμβάνοντες ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνικῶν (mēden lambanontes apo tōn ethnikōn)

p: By supporting the missionaries, those who stay at home become workers in the mission too.
b: Synergoi ginōmetha tē alētheia: "that we become fellow workers for the truth." Plummer argued that in the New Testament one is a fellow worker "of" a person, so the sense is "their fellow workers, for the truth": by supporting the brothers, Gaius and the Elder share their work. Others read "fellow workers with the truth," as if truth itself were at work. There is a play on words, which the Plain keeps: the brothers "take" (lambanontes) nothing from pagans (1:7), so believers are bound to "take" them under their care (hypolambanein, "take up, support").

p: The name means "nourished by Zeus." Nothing more is known of him than these two verses.
b: Diotrephēs means "nourished by Zeus"; Raymond Brown called it "not a particularly common name" (An Introduction to the New Testament, 1997). All we know is in these two verses: he "loves to be first" in his church, rejected the Elder's letter and his people, spoke against him, refused to receive the traveling brothers, and drove out of the church those who did. The Elder does not call him a false teacher. What his position was, and what the quarrel was about, are discussed on the chapter page. Diotrephes became a byword: an English Puritan, John Udall, gave his name to a proud bishop in a 1588 dialogue.

p: Philoprōteuō occurs only here. It recalls Jesus' saying about the one who wishes to be first.
b: Ho philoprōteuōn, "the one who loves being first," is found nowhere else in the New Testament. Plummer heard in it Jesus' warning: "And if anyone among you wishes to be first, he will be your slave" (Matthew 20:27; compare Mark 10:44). He suggested that Diotrephes wanted to make his church independent of the Elder, "to his own glorification." Whether he held an office is not said.

p: Epidechomai means "receive, accept." In 1:10 the same verb means refusing the brothers hospitality.
b: The verb epidechetai comes twice: Diotrephes "does not welcome us" (1:9) and "does not welcome the brothers" (1:10). Plummer thought that in 1:9 it may mean he would not accept the Elder's authority or his letter, and in 1:10 that he refused the brothers hospitality, or that he "closes his doors" in both places. "Us" may include the Elder's people; by not saying "me," the Elder avoids making it a personal quarrel.

a: babbling against us with evil words
p: Phlyareō means to talk nonsense. The Elder calls Diotrephes' accusations both wicked and silly.
b: Phlyareō means "talk nonsense, prattle"; Plummer notes it is common in Aristophanes and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. The related noun describes the idle young widows of 1 Timothy 5:13, who "chatter and meddle." "Evil" here is ponēros, the word for "the evil one" in 1 John. When he comes, the Elder will "point out" these works (hypomnēsō, literally "call to mind"); Plummer explains, "I will direct public attention to the matter."
orig: λόγοις πονηροῖς φλυαρῶν ἡμᾶς (logois ponērois phlyarōn hēmas)

a: drives them out of the church
p: Ekballō is the word used when the man born blind was driven out of the synagogue in John 9.
b: Ek tēs ekklēsias ekballei: Diotrephes "drives out of the church" those who want to receive the brothers. The same verb is used in John 9:34-35: "And they drove him out." Whether this was a formal expulsion, which would show Diotrephes had real authority, or pressure that forced people to leave, is not clear (Plummer: "we have not sufficient knowledge of the circumstances"). The present tenses suggest it was still going on.
orig: ἐκ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἐκβάλλει (ek tēs ekklēsias ekballei)

a: do not imitate the bad, but the good
p: Kakos, "bad," is a different word from ponēros, "evil," in 1:10. The Plain keeps them apart.
b: The Elder turns from Diotrephes to a general rule. He uses to kakon, "the bad," a common Greek word that John rarely uses, rather than ponēros, "evil" (1:10) (Plummer). The Plain marks the change with "bad" and "evil." "Imitate" (mimeomai) is the verb of 2 Thessalonians 3:7, 9 and Hebrews 13:7: believers learn by copying good examples, and the next verse offers one, Demetrius.
orig: μὴ μιμοῦ τὸ κακὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀγαθόν (mē mimou to kakon alla to agathon)

p: No one has seen God (John 1:18), but in John's letters doing good shows that a person knows him.
b: "Nobody has ever seen God" (John 1:18). Yet 1 John says that the one who sins has not seen God or known him (1 John 3:6), and that whoever does not love the brother he has seen cannot love the God he has not seen (1 John 4:20). In the same way, "anyone who does good is from God": a person's actions show where he comes from (1 John 3:10). The Elder applies the rule to the choice in front of Gaius, between Diotrephes' way and Demetrius'.

p: Probably the bearer of this letter. 3 John may be, in part, his letter of recommendation.
b: Nothing else is known of Demetrius. Plummer thought he was perhaps the bearer of the letter, and many read 3 John as, in part, a letter of recommendation for him (C. H. Dodd), like Paul's for Phoebe (Romans 16:1-2: "Let me recommend to you Phoebe, our sister"). A letter of recommendation of about AD 25 from Egypt names its bearer in the same way: "Heraclides, the bearer of this letter, is my brother" (Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 292). That he is the silversmith of Ephesus who made shrines of Artemis (Acts 19:24) is a guess Plummer thought "worth mentioning" but not probable. The Apostolic Constitutions (about 380) list him as bishop of Philadelphia.

p: How can truth testify? The Elder may mean Demetrius' life matches the truth, or that the Spirit of truth bears witness.
b: Plummer found two explanations the best. (1) "The truth" is the rule believers walk by, and Demetrius' life so plainly fits it that the rule itself testifies for him. (2) "The truth" is the Spirit of truth (1 John 5:6), who guides the believers who speak well of him, as in John 15:26-27, where the Spirit testifies and the disciples testify too. Plummer preferred the second. Two early copies read "by the church" instead (see the variant).
orig: ὑπὸ αὐτῆς τῆς ἀληθείας (hypo autēs tēs alētheias)

a: you know our testimony is true
p: The Gospel of John ends with the same claim: "we know his testimony is true."
b: The Greek oidas hoti hē martyria hēmōn alēthēs estin is very close to John 21:24: "This disciple is the one giving testimony about these events... And we know his testimony is true" (compare John 19:35). Plummer reports Westcott's suggestion that John 21:24 may be an echo of this sentence. "You know" is singular in the oldest copies; the Byzantine text has the plural, and a few copies read "we know," under the influence of John 21:24.
orig: οἶδας ὅτι ἡ μαρτυρία ἡμῶν ἀληθής ἐστιν (oidas hoti hē martyria hēmōn alēthēs estin)

p: 2 John says "paper and ink"; 3 John says "ink and pen." The pen (kalamos) was a cut reed.
b: Kalamos is a reed, cut to a point and used as a pen (Plummer); elsewhere in the New Testament it means a reed plant or a measuring rod (Matthew 11:7; Revelation 11:1). The ending of 3 John (1:13-14) runs almost word for word with 2 John 1:12, which shows the two letters were written about the same time (Plummer). The Plain matches the two where the Greek is the same and differs where it differs: "I have" and "I had," "I chose not" and "I do not want," "paper and ink" and "ink and pen."
orig: διὰ μέλανος καὶ καλάμου (dia melanos kai kalamou)

p: In the Greek editions "Peace to you" starts verse 15. English Bibles following the KJV count fourteen verses.
b: The KJV, which this site follows for verse numbers, ends 3 John at verse 14. The SBL Greek text, which the site translates, splits the verse and numbers "Peace to you. The friends send you greetings. Greet each of the friends by name" as verse 15. Nothing is missing; only the numbering differs. "Peace to you" (eirēnē soi) is the Hebrew greeting shalom, the words of the risen Jesus: "Peace to you" (John 20:19; John 20:26). It takes the place of the ordinary letter's "Farewell."

a: Greet each of the friends by name
p: Jesus called his disciples friends, and the good shepherd calls his sheep "each by name."
b: "The friends" (hoi philoi) is unusual: elsewhere believers are "brothers." Jesus said, "I have called you friends" (John 15:15), and Plummer suggests the word suits a private letter. Some copies change it to "brothers" (see the variant). Kat' onoma, "by name," occurs in the New Testament only here and in John 10:3, where the shepherd "calls out to his own sheep, each by name." The Elder wants each friend greeted personally, as a shepherd knows his flock.
